basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-12 from the published page (posts/part-4-intro/index.md, 479 words by check_draft's count, ten units: four lead paragraphs, five chapter paragraphs and 'Begin with ...') and its former spec.md, then reordered the same day (see decision_log); the page was revised to match. know: Part IV answers five questions in order: what the warehouse system must receive and report, how carriers are connected and a delivery date computed, what a store adds and how its cross-channel services work, how a return moves money and stock, and how the customer and the agent learn the order's status.
After checkout, the physical facts (stock on the shelf, the parcel's whereabouts, store stock, what came back) are known first by the system on the spot.

Part I: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines (money, goods, returns), system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation; the glosses for WMS, ERP, POS, 3PL, iPaaS, OMS and webhook; the Waypoint program and its decisions W1 to W8; the incidents in outline.

Parts II and III: available-to-promise and one writer each for on hand and committed; checkout creating the order once; refunds as new payments with one writer; one order record with three status lines; one invoice per shipment.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can name the five chapters' subjects in reading order.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only this page: what will each of the next five chapters tell you, in order?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The instruction and response between order management and the warehouse; carrier integration and credible delivery dates; the store's till as a source of orders, stock and customer records; the return request, inspection, stock decision and refund as separate steps with owners; notifications, the status page and the support view built from shared facts.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can say why a shop can promise 'tomorrow' and deliver a day later although nobody was slow.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: why was Eva promised Wednesday and delivered Thursday, and what should the promise have been based on?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A static storefront rule ignored the warehouse's timing: her order came after the last dispatch work of the day. The promise should be computed from the warehouse's collection schedule and backlog, the stock's location and the carrier's performance, not written as a sentence.

thesis.question: Once the order is placed, how are the promises made about it (a delivery date, a collection, a return and its refund, the status the customer sees) kept?
thesis.claim: Promises about a placed order are kept only where each physical fact has one system that witnesses and writes it (the warehouse system, the store's till, the carrier, the returns bench) and that applies each instruction once, as a keyed request it accepts or rejects; where each promise is computed from that system's events or released by its confirmation; and where the customer and the service agent read one status built from those events.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that fulfillment is operations' work rather than architecture: once checkout has taken the order and the money, promises are kept by enough pickers, reliable carriers and helpful agents, and the storefront's delivery sentence, the shop platform's order status and its default refund flow are enough.
thesis.so_what: Kestrel & Pine's four Part IV incidents were promises made without the witness's facts or acted on by more than one system: the Queue That Waited (roughly 8,000 Black Friday orders missed next-day delivery while the page promised it), the Store Stock Mirage (37 collection items already sold), the Double Refund (212 returns, €19,400) and the Three-Status Order (11 tickets). A merchant that accepts the claim names the witness and the writer of each physical fact, and the event each promise reads, before it buys a faster warehouse, a new till or more service capacity.
thesis.how_why: The storefront promises in seconds; the physical work happens hours or days later in buildings and vans the order record cannot see, and its facts (an empty pick location, a unit sold at the till, a parcel scan, a worn jacket on the bench) are known first by the system on the spot and reach the others by message, late or twice. A promise read from a copy or a static sentence is wrong whenever the copy lags or the queue grows; a status set by one integration overwrites what others know; and an action that two systems can take, such as a refund, is taken twice.

supporting_claims.claim: Each physical fact has one system that witnesses it and is its only writer: the warehouse system for on-hand stock at the warehouse, the till for store stock and store sales, the carrier's scans for the parcel's whereabouts and the returns bench's disposition for what came back; every other system holds a copy fed by that system's events.

The order record instructs the place that does the work through a fulfillment order that the place accepts or rejects and that carries a key, so a repeated instruction creates no second pick; after acceptance a cancellation or an edit is a request the place answers, and self-service and agents' actions check that state first.

A promise about time or place is computed from the warehouse's cut-off, capacity and backlog, the stock's location and the carrier's measured transit time per lane, with a buffer and a margin, and a promise against store stock becomes a commitment only when a person at the store confirms it.

On the way back, the warehouse's disposition is the event that releases the refund and the restock, and one system issues the refund with the return id as its key, whether the return started in the portal, at a store counter or on a marketplace.

The customer and the agent see one status, derived from these events and kept in one order record as separate goods (per shipment), money and return states; the notifications, the status page and the agent's view are read models over that record.

flow.rationale: The page opens where Part III left the order (recorded and paid) on the gap between a confirmation in seconds and physical work that can slip a day, and narrows to Eva's one jacket out and back, delivered a day late, then to the company she bought from and its volumes; it then widens once, from her order to who knows each physical fact first and the three rules that follow for every order (with Figure 2, which pictures the systems), then gives the roadmap in its own paragraph, before narrowing again to one paragraph per chapter in the order of Eva's parcel, each opening on one case, with Figure 3 after them mapping the named incidents onto the promises; it ends by naming the cause of the opening's day-late delivery and sending the reader to the warehouse. Eva's order comes directly after the opening because it is the sequence the opening describes; the company comes after her order because it is where she bought; the rules come after both because they name the places her order passes through; Figure 3 comes after the chapter list because its caption names incidents the chapter paragraphs introduce. flow.rationale: Each chapter uses what the one before it fixed. The warehouse comes first because it defines the fulfillment order, the warehouse system as the writer of on-hand stock, and the cut-off, capacity and backlog; the shipping chapter computes the delivery promise from those three and adds the carrier's events and one vocabulary for them; the stores chapter reuses the fulfillment order, labels and carrier pickup for ship-from-store and the computed promise for collection, and adds the till as a second witness of stock and orders; the returns chapter needs the carrier's 'delivered' event, which starts the 14-day clock, the warehouse's receiving and stock events, and the store-return rule the stores chapter set, and adds the returns bench's disposition as the witness of what came back; the service chapter comes last because its messages, status page and agent view read the events every earlier chapter defined. Putting shipping before the warehouse would ask the reader to compute a promise from a cut-off and backlog not yet explained; putting stores before shipping would describe ship-from-store and the collection promise before labels, carrier pickup and the computed promise exist; putting returns before stores would leave its store-return section pointing forward; putting service earlier would describe messages for events whose emitters the reader has not met and would leave the part without the chapter that joins its events into one status.
